title: Longitudinal Refusal Rate Tracking on a Fixed Prompt Set Across Model Versions

original_idea.title: Longitudinal Refusal Rate Tracking on a Fixed Prompt Set Across Model Versions
original_idea.problem: Model updates happen frequently but safety property changes are not systematically tracked. A longitudinal study using archived model versions can reveal whether fine-tuning or RLHF steps change refusal behavior in predictable ways.
original_idea.direction: Use Hugging Face model version history for a model with multiple public checkpoints (e.g., Mistral or Llama variants fine-tuned over time). Run a fixed set of 50–100 safety prompts on each checkpoint. Plot refusal rate, response length, and harm score over versions. Identify whether safety regressions follow capability improvements.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Post-deployment safety tracking is an open problem. Using already-available model checkpoints makes this feasible without needing API access or special permissions.
original_idea.relevant_context: The FLI AI Safety Index criticizes companies for lacking monitoring and control mechanisms. Hugging Face hosts many historical checkpoints publicly, making this experiment low-cost.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: tracking safety regressions across model versions directly informs deployment monitoring and release practices. The finding would be immediately useful for practitioners.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires downloading multiple model checkpoints and running inference on each. Medium compute needed for multiple model versions. Setup complexity is moderate but not beginner-trivial.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multiple checkpoints of a model family means multiple inference runs. Scope depends on how many checkpoints exist. Could be narrowed to 3-4 checkpoints but still substantial.

novelty.reasoning: Some longitudinal tracking exists — RefusalBench and the Refusal Index protocol provide methodology. Research has shown refusal dropping from 25% to 0% across three model generations within one family. SORRY-Bench provides a fine-grained taxonomy for measuring refusal. However, a systematic study using Hugging Face public checkpoints of a specific model family (e.g., Mistral or Llama variants) with a fixed prompt set tracking safety regression over fine-tuning versions is not fully published. The methodology exists but the specific application to publicly-available checkpoint histories is a practical contribution.
